content.thinking:
I'm planning the dragonbone soul scythe's design — standing upright on a small plinth, around 2.1 meters total height, with the staff rising vertically and only the moving parts needing joints.

I need a root joint since the builder requires one, plus maybe a hinge joint for a hanging charm or soul-flame tassel to keep it visually interesting but simple. I'm mapping out the layout: the blade oriented in the X-Y plane for a readable silhouette from the front, with thickness along Z, and the plinth built as a stepped lathe shape with the staff rising from its top.

Now I'm plotting the staff and scythe head proportions—total height around 2.25 with the head positioned near the top, the blade sweeping outward toward +X and curving downward to a tip around (0.95-1.15, -0.1 to -0.45) relative to the head origin. I'm defining the blade's outline as two curves, a thicker spine on top and the cutting edge below, meeting at the tip to form the crescent shape, and working out the point ordering so the geometry closes correctly.

Checking that the tip and edge segments don't cross — the edge curve stays on the correct interior side near the tip, so the outline should be non-self-intersecting. I'll avoid heavy smoothing to prevent corner-cutting from introducing a crossing, so I'll set smoothing to 0.

Going with a faceted, low-poly angular look to match the sharp League-style blade aesthetic. For the double-thick spine, I'll use a small bevel (0.005) to keep it crisp without risking shrink errors. For the glowing edge, I'm planning a thin inset strip or sweep along the edge curve points to create a soul-fire cyan-teal glow effect along the blade.

Now I'm working out the blade's coloring with a custom gradient paint that blends from bone-ivory at the spine to teal glow at the edge, using the extrude cross-section coordinates to drive the mix, then wrapping it in a cel-shaded toon paint for that stylized look.

Still defining edge coloring logic...

For the lighting, the extrude faces point along ±Z and the key light sits at +z, so the front face gets lit while the back falls into shadow, which the cel-shading wrapper handles through the paint resolver. Flat color budget stays fine since paints don't count against it, and now I'm thinking the dragonbone staff could be a spinal column with vertebrae discs placed along the twisted core using a path-following helper.

For each vertebra I'm planning small cylinder discs plus spike-shaped spinous processes oriented along the path tangent, building them directly rather than merging geometry since the part count stays well under budget at roughly 100 parts. I just need to make sure each segment gets explicitly assigned to the root bone, since a literal path has no bone context and would otherwise fall back to the nearest joint.

Rather than using a curved path, I'll build the staff as a straight vertical rod with vertebrae discs spaced along it, adding backward spinous cone spikes and alternating side transverse process spikes at each disc.

Below the grip zone I'm wrapping dark leather bands and attaching a hanging charm joint with a chain leading to a small skull charm and glow orb for the soul-ribbon detail.

For the staff's head, I'm designing a collar socket with claw prongs gripping the blade base, topped with a dragon skull ornament — considering orientation so the blade reads clearly from a top-down view, with the skull's snout and glowing eye sockets positioned for best silhouette readability.

I'll have the skull face +Z with the blade emerging sideways from the cranium, letting the sphere-shaped skull naturally swallow the blade root; I'm placing the cranium sphere, snout box, lower jaw, and a pair of horns sweeping back from the top on each side.

For overall proportions, I'm aiming the skull top near 2.11 and horns up to 2.25, with the blade's outline reaching roughly 2.22 at the top, keeping total height around 2.25 meters and the weapon length near 2.2 meters — scythe-like but balanced. I'll break symmetry with a smaller curved bone spike counterweight on the opposite side, and scatter a few small teal soul-wisp shapes floating near the blade for atmosphere.

I'm adding a glowing forehead gem and planning rune decals on the blade faces, placing mirrored texture planes on front and back so the glyphs read correctly from both viewing angles.

For the rune texture itself, I'm sketching cyan glyph strokes on a transparent SVG canvas, then figuring out where a flat glyph plane can sit within the blade's curved silhouette — checking the spine and edge spans at different u positions so the plane stays fully inside the blade shape without poking out.

Now I'm working out the plane's world position and thickness offset from the blade's local coordinates, and considering whether the blade's thickness should taper linearly from thin at the edge to thick near the spine, based on the outline's y-range from tip to spine top.

Now I'm designing the plinth: a hexagonal stepped stone base with gold rim and a glowing rune ring, sized to socket the staff bottom. I'm also settling on a LoL-style palette—bone, dark purple-black, gold trim, and teal soul fire—to carry through the design.

Rounding out the plinth, I plan gold trim collars using torus rings along the staff, oriented on the Z axis at specific heights. I'm setting up a small helper function to place parts with typed options, importing the PartOptions type to keep everything consistent.

Now I'm defining the joint hierarchy, placing a root joint at the origin and adding a "charm" hinge joint near the top of the staff so the dangling charm can swing naturally from a ring attachment point.

I'm detailing the hanging charm itself: a gold chain segment, a small skull charm with glowing eyes, and a flowing ribbon sweep tapering downward in purple cel-shaded cloth material.

Then I'm working out the staff anatomy — mapping vertebra zones above and below the cloth-wrapped grip area, with each vertebra built as a short cylindrical disc using bone-colored cel shading.

Each vertebra also gets a small backward-pointing neural spine cone and two sideways transverse process cones, repeated across roughly twenty segments for about eighty small parts, with flat colors used on the tiny bits to keep things efficient. Between vertebrae I'm leaving gaps where the dark rod core shows through like intervertebral spacing.

For the grip, I'm planning a dark leather cylinder with gold banding at the ends, purple cloth wraps, and a gold pommel cap with a claw foot near the bottom, then I'll move on to assembling the skull at the staff's top.

Now I'm shaping the skull: a gold flared collar at the neck socket, a scaled sphere for the cranium, and a tapering frustum snout colored bone, working toward the upper jaw next.

Adding teeth cones and jaw joint...

Now placing nostrils and brow ridges, with dark eye sockets holding glowing orbs positioned at the front sides of the cranium, checking the socket coordinates fit within the cranium's ellipsoid bounds.

Then I'm sculpting horns as curved bone-colored sweeps rising from the cranium using Catmull-Rom paths with tapering radius, plus smaller secondary horns lower near the cheeks.

Adding a crest of spines along the back of the skull, then working on a gold collar bracket where the blade meets the cranium, being careful not to obscure the glyph region on the blade.

I'm adding small bone spike cones along the spine, computing outward normals from the segment tangents so they point up and away, with extra interpolated samples per segment for density.

I'm also adding wing-like rib rods running from spine to blade edge at scaled-down thin radii, offset slightly in z so they sit visibly on the surface rather than sinking into it.

Settling on a periodic modulo condition along a diagonal direction to fake rib grooves cheaply, restricted to the blade's upper, flatter region. Then moving on to the soul edge glow—a thin glowing sweep wrapping the blade's outer rim at the actual edge thickness.

Now I'm adding glow to the sweep and placing soul wisps along the blade's concave side—each a small glowing sphere with a flame-like tail and tiny dark dot eyes, positioned near the blade's curve toward the tip.

Each wisp gets a flame-shaped head with a curved downward tail spike, plus tiny dark eyes and a mouth for a ghostly face, with heads glowing brighter than the shadowed faces. I'm also adding a thin glowing rune ring around the plinth top with alternating tick marks encircling it.

For the plinth itself, I'm lathing a hexagonal stone profile with a stepped rim, painting it in mottled stone tones, then adding a gold band and under-glow slits for extra detail at the base.

Now I'm figuring out the claw cradle—three dragon claws curving upward from the plinth at 120-degree intervals, gripping the staff shaft between heights of 0.14 and 0.45, with each claw's base and tip positions defined by angle-based coordinates.

I'm also planning the vertebrae placement along the staff: clusters in two zones (roughly y=0.3–0.72 and y=1.3–1.8) spaced about 0.07 apart, adjusting counts so the claws' grip area has reasonable overlap with the lowest vertebrae.

Now I'm adding a wing-spar crossguard beneath the skull—two bone "wing" sweeps curving down and outward from the collar near y=1.82–1.84, tapering out to around y=1.66, checked against the blade root position so nothing overlaps awkwardly, then mirrored across the x-axis for symmetry.

I'll also add a counter-spike on the opposite side—a curved bone spur sweeping back from the skull with a tapering ridge and a gold ring at its base—plus gold filigree detailing like torus rings banding the staff at the grip ends, and runic textures for surface detail.

A glowing octahedral soul gem positioned at the forehead, slightly stretched and emissive, gives the skull a focal point. For the rune glyphs, I'll draw angular stroke paths as SVG shapes with cyan glow, sized to keep stroke widths crisp.

I'm reasoning through the mirroring for the back-facing plane and confirming it reads correctly despite the flip, then working out the exact placement and sizing of the glyph plane relative to the blade's spine and edges.

For a decorative gold inlay rod along the blade's spine, I'm calculating safe radius and offset positions so it stays proud of the surface rather than sinking into it, factoring in how blade thickness varies along its length.

Simplifying the spine nodes into a shorter list with a slight vertical offset, I'll sweep the inlay path as a polyline through those points, letting the skin rounding smooth the corners naturally. Now I'm defining the cel-shaded paint colors for the bone material, setting warmer shadow tones for the lit and dark variants.

Still defining paints...

I need helper functions for edge and spine positions along the blade, and I'm checking that the color types allow both flat strings and Paint objects for fills. Importing the glow effect for flat-colored parts and setting up the builder with the root joint and a helper for adding parts with typed color inputs.

Setting up imports...

Still defining blade outline points...

I'm writing an interpolation helper to find y-values along the spine and edge curves, then using that in the blade's paint function to compute a gradient based on distance from the edge, coloring points near the edge pale and shifting color further in.

Still writing shading logic...

Adding spike geometry details...

Still working out skull geometry...

Adding a small jaw hinge box, connecting the lower frustum into the cranium, and placing a tiny glowing soul-fire sphere between the jaws for visual flair. I'm also sketching spike fins on the sides of the cranium to suggest ears.

Now I'm defining the grip cylinder with spiral torus straps wrapped at intervals, plus the vertebra segments stacked along the staff with varying spacing in the lower and upper zones.

I'm adding the staff rod itself with dark flat-capped geometry, placing gold eyelet rings at key points like the grip ends and collar, and sketching purple cloth ribbon tails hanging down from the skull collar.

For the ribbons, I'm building curved catmull-rom paths that taper in radius toward the tip and blend into a teal gradient near the end, using box cross-sections with flat caps and proper orientation along the sweep.

Now I'm adding a glowing torus ring around the plinth's base at the right height, plus twelve small glowing rune tick-marks arranged radially around it, nudging their vertical position slightly above the plinth top to avoid z-fighting with the staff.

Switching to the hex plinth geometry, I'm checking whether the ring radius fits inside the hex's inradius so it doesn't poke through the flats, bumping the lathe segment count to twelve for smoother shading, then adjusting the ring and tick radii accordingly and setting the plinth base radius.

Now I'm defining a wisp-generating function that spawns a small glowing spherical head plus a tapered glowing tail spike extending outward from a given position, scaled and colored to match the soul glow.

I'm placing two tiny dark eye spheres offset on the head and confirming glow works correctly on swept geometry parts. I'm also tallying up the rough part count across vertebrae, teeth, wisps, spikes, ticks, and claws to make sure the total stays manageable, then setting up the jaw joint with its parent and aim positions.

Writing tuple geometry data...

Now I'm defining the blade extrusion with a tapered thickness profile and capped bevel, then setting up the rune glyph plane with its texture, size, and back-facing orientation.

I'm placing bolt studs as small spheres on the gold plates, sizing the plates to sit flush against the blade's taper at that point, and checking that the glyph plane doesn't overlap the plate region.

Now I'm checking the plate edges against the spine's taper to make sure the plate doesn't poke above or hang below the blade's silhouette, adjusting its center and height until the edges stay within bounds at both ends.

Still positioning the gold plate geometry...

Setting three bolts per side at varying z-heights, then checking the metadata export fields and verifying function signatures for the spike and sweep helpers—confirming the sweep accepts a polyline built from an array of point vectors with the right radius and options structure.

Writing vertebra function...

Still placing spikes...

Now I'm checking which imports are actually used before writing the file, confirming gradient, catmull, polyline, svg, and other helpers are all needed. I'm also setting up a hinge joint for a charm attachment near the root bone.

Positioning the charm details now: a gold eyelet torus fitted snug against the staff's grip, a thin gold chain rod hanging down, and a small skull charm made from a scaled sphere with a jaw box and eye sockets attached below it.

Then I'm adding a tail ribbon that sweeps down from the charm toward a glowing tip bead, with a purple-to-teal color gradient along its length—nudging its x-offset outward a bit so it doesn't clip into the grip's surface.
